The algorithm takes advantage of a compressive sensing technique to reconstruct the spectrum at each energy bin, resulting in an initial guess that is then refined using the PADIE method. Compared to existing techniques, this new approach enhances the reconstruction of energy spectra in x-ray scattering experiments. It has been tested on simulated data with multiple Compton scattering components and a range of limited scattering angles, achieving a 5-fold improvement in signal-to-noise ratio when reconstructing Compton spectra in energy bins of 10 eV, as well as refining reconstructed spectra with the help of theoretical Compton scattering profiles.

This research introduces a variation of the standard Darcy-Brinkman-Pressure equation (DBPE) to effectively capture blocking fractures resulting from the interaction of fractures and their surrounding porous media. The proposed model employs asymptotic single-particle resistance (ASPR) theory to represent the effects of fractures on the media's permeability, incorporating the $\beta$-function approach to model diverse fracture-media interactions. Numerical testing with blocking fractures, both in a simplified one-dimensional domain and a two-dimensional complex geometry, demonstrates the proposed model's capability to replicate blocking fractures and accurately capture their influence on flow and pressure fields. Compared to alternative approaches, the model exhibits superior performance in retaining physical coherence and predicting blocking fractures with asymptotic single-particle resistance, showing promise for modeling extensive blocking fractures in porous media.

Hypothesis selection is a fundamental problem in machine learning that's often tackled using model selection criteria such as AIC and BIC. These criteria rely on a utility function that balances model fit and complexity, but their behavior is largely understood in ideal scenarios. In practice, utility functions play a crucial role in decision-making, yet their impact and variability are not well characterized when data is flawed or multiple models are available. This paper delves into an exploratory analysis of utility functions, examining their optimal hypothesis, the effect of data quality, and how they influence the AIC/BIC-based hypothesis that is selected. We also study the relationship between utility functions and the AIC/BIC spectrum, finding that they can either favor simpler models, the AIC/BIC equilibrium, or more complex models. Furthermore, we show that the AIC/BIC-based hypothesis is the unique solution in special cases, and the AIC/BIC spectrum can serve as a section that defines utility functions, analogous to how the real numbers are defined by rational numbers. We support our theoretical findings with numerical experiments conducted using linear regression, group Lasso, and a hierarchical Poisson model.

Identifying discourse markers is crucial for grasping a text's overall meaning. Yet, accurate classification of these indicators has been hindered by the scarcity of well-annotated data. Such limitations are particularly pronounced in English, where accurate classification against a wide set of categories has remained unachieved. Our key contribution addresses this challenge by introducing a large dataset, spanning 20 categories and encompassing 20,000 labeled words of context, which is a significant step ahead of previous datasets. Furthermore, this dataset surpasses previous standards by featuring precise annotations of semantic relations, a feature we believe to be unparalleled in the field. To evaluate the effectiveness of our dataset, three baseline models were trained and tested on its contents. The results indicate areas for improvement in current techniques for predicting discourse categories based on context, as well as areas for advancement in DiscSense, a promising resource with considerable potential for contribution to related research areas.

We analyze the geometric properties of the factorized objective function in a specific matrix optimization problem, which involves a geodesic convex relaxation. The relaxation is defined on the set of symmetric positive-definite matrices and uses the Cholesky factorization as its constraint. To investigate the geodesic properties of the relaxed objective function, we establish conditions on the parameter of interest that guarantee the restricted strong convexity and smoothness of the relaxed objective function. These conditions enable us to compare the geodesic distances between different points in the relaxed convex body. As a result, we can determine when the geodesic convex relaxation has a non-negative geodesic curvature, which has implications for its numerical efficiency. We also develop a gradient method for minimizing the relaxed objective function, which has a specific form that ensures the non-negativity of the geodesic curvature of its iterate sequence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a specific matrix optimization application, which is crucial in designing learning algorithms for neural networks, particularly multilayer neural networks. In this example, we can precisely characterize the geodesic curvature of the relaxed objective function, which allows us to efficiently minimize the relaxation and accurately estimate the generalization performance of the network. We compare our approach with other widely used optimization methods, including the natural gradient method and ADMM, which can be challenging to apply to this specific problem due to their sensitivity to the precision of the matrix inverse operator and the inefficiency of dynamic memory allocation,

In 1990, Vizing proposed a conjecture that a bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 can be colored using 3 edges in a way that each vertex has the same edge degree. However, no proof or counterexample has been found for over three decades. Recently, a variation of this conjecture was confirmed for a specific class of bipartite graphs known as odd cycles. The current study aims to contribute to this topic by presenting algorithms that correctly color edges of odd cycles, achieving the desired edge degree of 2 for all vertices, or a degree of 3 for specific vertex sets, and providing examples of bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 for which no 3-edge coloring exists that meets the specified edge degree criteria.

This study investigates co-evolutionary genetic algorithms with two learning methods: social and individual learning. The research focuses on a game where two agents strive to find a common target by generating random Nash Equilibria, with the hamming distance serving as the performance indicator. The analysis compares social and individual learning through graph-based models, revealing distinct trends for expected Hamming distance in both scenarios. Specifically, social learning exhibits an exponential decline in expected Hamming distance, in contrast to individual learning which displays a linear increase. Additionally, the research reveals that social learning outperforms individual learning, while both learning approaches can be improved with varying population sizes and mutation rates.

Consider an oriented graph that contains weighted edges and is represented in a specific format. If this graph adheres to a specific standard, its edge ideal will exhibit two equivalent properties when considering two different ways of taking power operations. These two ways of taking power operations, known as ordinary and symbolic power, will result in ideals that are equal in both their contents and structure. This phenomenon can be seen as edge ideal coherence for this type of graph, which provides a significant condition for determining a specific dimensionality question. The paper also explores connections to previously established results, particularly in unweighted oriented graph settings, and presents a step towards investigating another dimensionality question.

Quantization-based neural network compression reduces data corruption risks by limiting input values to a specific range. However, applying non-uniform range restriction techniques to increase efficiency may compromise the network's performance. Our research introduces two methods, one linear and one non-linear, that modify model weights to accommodate a wider range of inputs while minimizing data corruption. The first approach uses weight scaling, demonstrating an efficient solution for limiting data ranges, particularly for small-scale models. In contrast, the second method, a non-linear model known as Residual Permutation Network (RPN), effectively handles larger, complex models, such as ResNet-50 and BERT. RPN's performance is comparable to the uncompressed model, making it a promising technique for compressing large neural networks.

This study examines two variations of the Jordanian twist: a higher-order version and a modified version. The general structure of the former is found to resemble the simple Jordanian twist, whereas the latter's structure serves as the basis for the former. Both twists are applied to the Lepowski-Zirke form of the Yang-Baxter operator in order to generate non-ultralocal integrable systems. The resulting systems from both approaches demonstrate equivalent properties and displays the $r$ matrix's inherent characteristics.

Using transfer learning from medium to high language resources has been proven to be an effective method for enhancing performance in resource-poor settings. Though introducing English as a resource has shown some success in LWT tasks, using medium to high German as a resource has not been explored extensively. To bridge the gap, a novel approach called \emph{Pan-German} is proposed, combining medium to high German resources for modeling a super-sense, then applying it to low German resources. The evaluation shows that Pan-German enhances the baseline by $4.5\%$ in average F1-score, outperforming a direct English transfer to low German resources by approximately two times. Additionally, employing Pan-German resources reduces the performance difference between low and medium German resources to a notable extent, demonstrating its potential in helping medium German resources.

Our research analyzed the production of charged particles in high-energy collisions involving various systems, ranging from the smallest (Au+Au collisions at 54.4 GeV) to the largest (Pb+Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV); we compared particle ratios across these collisions. The collaborative effort combined data from the STAR experiment for Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, and the ALICE experiment for Pb+Pb collisions. The resulting data sets were analyzed within identical frameworks to ensure consistency. Charged particle transverse momentum spectra were re-calculated using a novel method that corrects for acceptance and efficiency losses in detectors; this approach yielded corrected spectra for all systems studied. We also calculated ratios of particle yields to charged particle pairs, known as inclusive particle ratios, which were calculated using a technique that accounts for biases in tracked particles. These ratios were calculated for various hadron species, including pions, kaons, protons, omega baryons, K-s mesons, Lambda baryons, and phi mesons; these ratios were calculated over a range of transverse momentum values from 0.2 GeV/c to 5 GeV/c for most systems, except for omega baryons and K-s mesons which were analyzed from 0.4 GeV/c to 5 GeV/c. We're taking a look at the influence that a city's infrastructure has on the spread of unrest, and to do this, we're using a model based on a simple transportation system. Previous research suggested that a change in a system's topology could cause a delay in the completion of a task, and we're building on this by exploring how this affects the activation of activists in different parts of the city. Once activated, they influence local communities in a way that can lead to a cascade of events, and we're using this process to examine the role that infrastructure plays in the timing and occurrence of these events. By simulating real-world scenarios, we found that faster transportation between areas can prevent the activation of activists in those areas, and that varying the layout of the city's infrastructure can significantly impact the delay in the completion of a task, as well as the activation of activists and the spread of unrest. We also found that the activation of activists and the unrest that follows can occur even if activists are never directly influenced, and that this unrest may reach a point of no return, leading to widespread societal collapse.

This paper presents a new method for verifying if one regular expression is contained within another. The key component in processing regular expressions for this verification process is Brzozowski's derivative operator. Theoretical evidence suggests this method results in a decision procedure that is closed under a specific class of representations, but lacks equivalence to regular expressions in sufficient generality for many practical applications. In contrast, the proposed technique utilizes Brzozowski's operator within a symbolic decision process that is now capable of checking containment within a set of regular expressions that is more extensive than previously known, and includes many expressions commonly found in practical scenarios.

This paper presents a novel approach to integrating lidar and camera sensors for state estimation in autonomous vehicles. A customized place recognition network is designed to leverage both sensors' data, incorporating their point clouds and images. The network's output is fed into an EKF-based VIO algorithm for state estimation and prediction. Unlike traditional VIO algorithms, this network-based solution treats data processing as a learned task, utilizing the network to determine suitable feature extraction methods. The system's performance was evaluated on raw data from real journeys, achieving navigation performance metrics of 0.23 px/cm and 0.54 deg/cm for position and orientation estimation, respectively. Furthermore, comparative testing demonstrated the system's efficacy when using separate place recognition and tracking networks.

A new theoretical model, incorporating both second- and third-order Weyl points, has been devised for a three-dimensional solid with a honeycomb-shaped unit cell, utilizing a three-layer atomic arrangement. This design incorporates a corkscrew pattern of atomic displacements to generate a large frequency dispersion around the third-order Weyl points at the zone center, enabling the direct visualization of Weyl electrons in a solid. A hypothetical material based on iridium and platinum has been proposed, with a predicted material parameter for phonon-mediated coupling of Weyl electrons, offering a potential explanation for the diversity of structural phases in materials and possibly revealing a new mechanism for Jahn-Teller distortion. Notably, this material exhibits a non-trivial connection between its electronic and elastic responses, evoking the concept of square-root topology, a novel aspect distinct from the well-known concept of elastic or acoustic square-root topology.

The effectiveness of edge finite elements is well established for solving various partial differential equations, particularly those involving smooth solutions. However, when dealing with the problem of completing partial data, where the partial information is missing in certain regions, the performance varies greatly. Recent studies have demonstrated issues with traditional edge elements in accurately resolving data in the interior of the domain. In contrast, discontinuous Galerkin methods with interface terms have shown better results. In this research, we investigate how different edge element finite element methods handle completing data in the presence of smooth interfaces. By analyzing the approximation properties, we show that methods with a narrower jump near interfaces are better at resolving data. Additionally, we provide numerical examples to demonstrate that choosing optimal methods, in conjunction with a finer mesh, can accurately recover data in the interior. Furthermore, unlike previous research, we encounter no difficulties with data resolution in the presence of smooth interfaces.

We present a novel method that makes use of explanations or saliency, allowing a less capable model to focus on correcting specific errors made by a more capable model, without requiring access to the model's training data. This technique, known as the ``saliency-based approach,'' facilitates the training of a student model to combine information with a teacher model, without the need for access to the model's underlying details. By redefining the target model output and introducing a new combination task that accounts for the teacher model's characteristics, the saliency-based approach delivers a student model that efficiently incorporates the knowledge from the teacher model, without suffering from a decline in performance due to overfitting. When combining disparate models, our method achieves significant improvements, with results showing that the saliency-based approach yields comparable or better results than baselines, including coarse teaching, explicit error correction, and selective attention, across a wide range of tasks and model capacity disparities.

We examine the family of number fields known as S4 quartic fields, which have the property that the Galois group of their Galois conjugates forms a group isomorphic to the symmetric group S4. We study these fields in relation to Diophantine equations involving cubic residues, specifically those of the form x^3 ≡ a (mod p). We establish an important connection between these equations and the rational points of certain elliptic curves. We establish bounds on the number of rational points of a specific curve,  y^2 = x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3), that do not belong to certain subfields of the S4 quartic fields. We achieve this by applying techniques from the area of Diophantine geometry, including those related to Faltings' theorem and its consequences. We demonstrate the applicability of these techniques by establishing upper limits on which primes can be included in our field inclusion criteria. We establish that all prime numbers less than 1000 can be included in our criteria, although this may not generally hold for a wider range of primes. We also establish that only a finite number of prime numbers can be included in our criteria as we vary the fixed parameter 'd' of our Diophantine equation. We demonstrate that this number is relatively small, on the order of 10^20, for a significant portion of the parameter 'd'. We investigate the dynamics of an isolated system with a finite number of systems whose classical degrees of entropy change over time are measured. Using the concept of relative entropy, we define the irreversible entropy produced during the process. We show that the change in entropy is directly related to the change in temperature, and we determine the relationship between the heat transferred and the change in temperature. We apply this approach to two specific scenarios: a quantum quench of a harmonic oscillator and a quench of N harmonic oscillators with mutual coupling. We study the dynamics of entropy production, find patterns in the dynamics of the system's degrees of freedom, and compare theoretical predictions with numerical data.

Quantifying the time it takes for a non-unitary dynamics to lead to distinguishability between two initially prepared states is crucial for understanding the longevity of quantum coherence. This time-dependent distinguishability can be analyzed by examining the twirling of the initial state-over-time with respect to a specific unitary transformation, although this requires a broad understanding of the dynamics. Here, we outline a more localized approach to determine the time-twirling of the initial state-over-time, which is equivalent to analyzing the twirling of the system's reduced dynamics alone. This is particularly useful for assessing the durability of quantum entanglement in noisy channels. Our novel strategy involves deriving two distinct operators, denoted as $\mathcal{D}_\gamma(\cdot | \rho_E)$ and $\Delta_\gamma(\cdot | \rho_E)$, which are derived from the system's reduced dynamics and provide distinct insights into the time-twirling of the initial state-over-time. These operators exhibit desirable properties, including being positive, trace-one operators, and are unaffected by the unitary twirling operation. They are also invariant under unitary twirling and demonstrate a minimum value of $1/d$ for a d-dimensional system, where the value becomes sharper with increasing time and depends on the system's initial state and environment. Our research also introduces two distinct measures of time-twirling, denoted as $\Pi_t$ and $\Delta_t$, which are directly linked to these operators and provide essential insights into the durability of quantum coherence

Let $n$ be a positive integer. A standard simplex in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called \emph{regular} if its vertices form the equidistant points from a common point inside the simplex. Let $Q_n$ denote the unit cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We are given $m$ points inside $Q_n$, not counting those on the edges of $Q_n$. Under the assumption that these $m$ points do not form a nondegenerate regular simplex, we want to find the smallest number of these points that must be placed on the edges of $Q_n$ in order to ensure they cannot form an edge of a nondegenerate regular simplex. In this paper, we will use the term \emph{edge-simplex} to describe a nondegenerate regular simplex whose vertices lie on the edges of $Q_n$. We will show that forming an edge-simplex is possible if and only if there are exactly $n+1$ points inside $Q_n$, not including those on the edges, which are equidistant from a common point inside the cube. To analyze the near-surface carrier concentration of cleaved and etched silicon, a non-invasive method using photoreflectance is proposed. Comparing this method to analyzing the etched buffer oxide layer above the silicon surface reveals that the carrier concentration in cleaved silicon is significantly higher, indicating the presence of space charge regions at the oxide-silicon interface. To further investigate, a model based on the semiconductor-oxide system is developed to interpret results and understand the impact of oxide etching on carrier concentration gradients in silicon.

We've analyzed the potential evolution of Venus's atmosphere, considering the exchange of mass and energy between the planet's surface, atmosphere, and orbital system over thousands to millions of years. Atmospheric cycling, which occurs through processes like atmospheric loss, solar wind interaction, and planetary oscillations, affects heat distribution and, in turn, temperature gradients and the atmospheric circulation pattern. These, in turn, impact tectonic activity, surface topography, and atmospheric evolution. We used a multi-component model that integrated multiple timescales, from short atmospheric cycles to long geophysical and planetary timescales, to better capture the complex relationships and reciprocal influences. By applying this model to Venus, we simulated the planet's evolution with various parameters, such as atmospheric escape rates and solar energy, which were informed by recent research, including data from NASA's Venus Express and Pioneer Venus Orbiter missions. The simulations revealed that atmospheric cycling could significantly influence atmospheric composition and temperature, leading to snowball Earth scenarios, and even geophysical barotropy could result from cycling, which may be consistent with some geological features observed on Venus.

This research introduces a nonlinear Hawkes model addressing interaction complexities in multiple-event processes. Contrary to traditional linear Hawkes models, nonlinear extensions, such as polynomial and threshold-based representations, are explored to analyze multiple-relationship scenarios. We derive an iPDE solver for the nonlinear Hawkes model and provide numerical examples to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

To analyze the performance of a magnetized plasma waveplate, researchers consider three key factors including the thickness required for a $\pi$ phase shift, the coherence length of the Faraday rotation, and the influence of a windowed geometry. Studies show that the thickness of a $\pi$ phase shift can vary from several centimeters to above one meter, which is determined by the largest of either the plasma frequency or the classical waveplate frequency, in relation to the window size in a windowed geometry. Additionally, in a windowed geometry, the coherence length of the Faraday rotation, which dictates the ability to modulate the phase, can be significantly shorter than desired, typically in the range of a few millimeters to over a hundred millimeters, and may be influenced by magnetic field strength and electron density. By comparing the necessary thickness of a $\pi$ phase shift to the coherence length of a windowed geometry, which can be experimentally determined, researchers can assess the waveplate's effectiveness even if the electron density and magnetic field strength are unknown.

We analyze the tau electric dipole moment in the type-II two-Higgs doublet extension of the Standard Model, considering all possible contributions from the Higgs sector. Taking into account the experimental constraints from the $B$ meson decay and the search for extra Higgs bosons, we calculate the expected range for the tau dipole moment, expressed in terms of its sensitivity to certain Higgs coupling products. This allows us to identify potential new directions for experimental searches, particularly for a scenario with a light charged Higgs boson. Moreover, we find that a significant lower bound can be placed on the tau dipole moment, with a predicted value likely exceeding $10^{-20}$ e.cm within the parameter space of interest. This prediction motivates future experiments to improve the sensitivity for the tau dipole moment to below $10^{-20}$ e.cm.

High-spin states in rare-earth doped solids are crucial for developing quantum reference frames and geometric quantum error correction. Rare-earth doped selenide halides are highly fluorescent and symmetric, making them ideal for this purpose, but their synthesis is not well understood. This work explores the synthesis methods, material properties, and symmetry of rare-earth doped Sr2NaGa5S11, a compound with which the authors have varying degrees of success. They find that this material can be synthesized with a high degree of symmetry when doped with neodymium, but with misshapen crystals when doped with praseodymium or erbium. The neodymium doped material exhibits unique error correction properties in its scattering patterns, indicating a connection between spin, light scattering, and quantum error correction.

We establish a connection between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator and the conserved current OPE block in CFT$_2$, demonstrating that this block corresponds to a $(1,1)$ representation in the CFT$_2$. Conversely, we show the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator can be expressed in terms of an AdS$_2$ geodesic operator, enabling the mapping of its associated CFT$_3$ block to a $(2,1)$ representation in CFT$_2$. This representation can be further related to the conserved current OPE block in CFT$_2$, extending previous understanding in a more comprehensive framework.

This work provides an updated formulation of the Serre-Swan theorem in the context of combinatorial differential manifolds, taking into consideration the perspectives of Daniel Gelfand and Mark MacPherson. Specifically, it shows that a combinatorial differential manifold can be accurately described as a set of points that correspond to the local components of a specific atlas, and these points possess specific properties including being torsors over the reals and adhering to certain consistency rules. Furthermore, it demonstrates that every combinatorial differential manifold contains the same topological information as a singular simplicial manifold and that this contains essentially the same information as a smooth simplicial manifold that can be recovered through the use of techniques related to the realization of rational functions. It also establishes the equivalence to another definition presented by Gelfand and MacPherson, which involves greater generality, although requiring the use of finite-dimensional vector spaces instead of just the reals.

The peculiar supernova SN~2020jfo has been studied using spectroscopic and photometric data, covering a period of about 108 days. Observations were collected from 10 to 119 days post-explosion and reveal a slow and broad H gamma absorption in early spectra that quickly disappeared, along with distinct absorption features of neutral Ni and Fe ions emerging around 30-40 days. The [NiI]/[FeII] ratio in SN~2020jfo is remarkably high, with a value 4 times greater than the solar nickel-iron ratio in the Earth's atmosphere. This unusual ratio remains high throughout the observation period, with a significant decrease in the [NiI]/[FeII] ratio in many other supernovae having the lowest 10-day $^{56}$Ni luminosity. Notably, the light curves of radio and X-ray emissions and the bolometric light curve of SN~2020jfo indicate a large amount of $^{56}$Ni, with a lower limit of 1.5 solar masses. The nebular phase spectra show the typical signs of supernova interacting with a massive circumstellar medium, with a large expansion velocity of [SII] lines and the absence of [ClII] and [ArII] lines.
